title: Let the sources fix what a definition grades
statement: Grade a concept only on features every authoritative source treats as defining, teaching usual ones as typical, and never build a wrong option on a sense any source accepts.
example: Of three features a first pass claimed for one literary term, checking glossaries left one that every source treats as defining.
detail: Research for a lesson on a literary term checked dictionaries and glossaries: a first pass claimed three features missing from the course's definition, and validation cut them to one that every source treats as defining (`othello-course-renderer-draft/repo/docs/research/g4-u1-l1-what-is-an-epic.md`, lines 125-129). Features only some sources list belong in the passage as what such works usually carry, never in the definition a child is graded against, and the lesson plan adopted that (lines 131-135; `othello-course-renderer-draft/repo/content/lesson-plans/g4-u1-l1.json`, line 483). The same research found a broad modern sense of the term accepted by some sources, so an option built on it is nearly right rather than wrong, while one built on "it just means very long" is fair (lines 215-219). The course's shipped intro video had already keyed that broad sense as a checkpoint's correct answer (the plan, line 483).

One caution for distractor writing: a broad modern sense of epic as simply a long heroic story is accepted by some sources, so "a long story about a hero" is nearly right rather than wrong. The wrong part is dropping the verse form, the people's stake and the gods, not the largeness. A distractor built on "it just means very long" is fair; one built on "a long story about a hero" is not.

Distractor consequence: a broad modern sense of epic as a long heroic story is accepted by some sources, so a long story about a hero is nearly right rather than wrong. It just means very long is a fair distractor; a long story about a hero is not.

**Not universal, so not assessable:** the fate of a whole people riding on the hero appears in Abrams' glossary but not in the Poetry Foundation's. Divine intervention appears in one of three glossaries, and there only as something that "frequently" happens. Both belong in the passage as what epics usually carry, never in the definition a child is graded against.
**Universal:** an epic is a long narrative **poem**. Every source checked treats that as definitional, and our definition drops it.
The first pass on this claimed three missing features. Validation cut it to one, and the one that survives is enough on its own.

Research section 5 puts the people's stake in what epics usually carry and explicitly not in "the definition a child is graded against", because it is not universal across the glossaries checked. So it is spoken, and it is not assessed, and neither the closing item nor either proposed in-video item keys on it.
